newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Firm tests Taiwan policy with China project.
newsitem.headline: Firm tests Taiwan policy with China project.

text.p: Taiwan's government will check on Formosa Plastics' unauthorised US$3 billion power project in China and punish the firm if necessary, Taiwan newspapers reported on Sunday.

The news came as the China Times quoted unidentified sources as saying the group may resume a US$6 billion petrochemical project in China which it suspended in 1992 under pressure from the Taiwan government.
Formosa officials were not immediately available for comment.

In mid-March, Taipei's economics ministry and related government offices urged local firms to stop making unauthorised investments in China and vowed to ferret out and punish illegal projects, despite evidence that Beijing was helping them keep a low profile.

The Economic Daily News on Sunday quoted Finance Minister Paul Chiu as saying his ministry would check the funding sources of Formosa's latest China investment, and vowed to punish it if there had been any violations of rules.
"Formosa Plastics' fund flows and procedures will be checked," Chiu was quoted as saying.
The China Times quoted vice-economics minister Yin Chi-ming as saying Formosa's China power project required special government approval, failing which it would be punished.
Authorities can impose fines, repeatedly if necessary, of T$3 million to T$15 million (US$110,000-US$550,000), the paper said.
However, business leaders have urged the government to adopt a flexible and feasible China investment policy.

The United Daily News quoted Kao Chin-yen, chief executive of President Enterprises, Taiwan's top mainland investor, as saying excessively tough restrictions on Taiwanese investments in China could prompt firms to go underground. This would make it even more difficult to control them, he added.

On Saturday the chairman of Formosa Plastics, Wang Yung-ching, confirmed that the group had started building a US$3 billion thermal power plant in China's coastal Fujian province despite not having Taipei's approval.
"(Formosa Plastics group) has begun construction (of the China project)," Wang said on state television.

It is was the first time Formosa had confirmed rumours that the group had started construction of the project. Previously, it had insisted that it would not go ahead with the project if the Taiwan government disagreed.
"Once (the construction) started, we cannot ... stop it. If the government disapproves it, we insist to wait and see whether the government policy can be changed," Wang said.

Wang added that if the government was not prepared to grant approval Formosa would not use funds from either its domestic member companies and its overseas affiliates, but may seek foreign funds instead.

In June 1996, the Formosa group, which includes Formosa Plastics, Nan Ya Plastics and Formosa Chemical and Fiber announced plans to build the $3 billion, 3,600-megawatt Fujian power plant in partnership with Fujian authorities.
The group applied for Taiwan state approval but publicly backed out two months later after Taiwan president Lee Teng-hui appealed to local enterprises to slow their investments on the mainland.
Taiwan investment must be routed through Hong Kong or other third parties and must have Taiwan government approval.

China regards Taiwan as a rebel-held province since a civil war split them in 1949. However, nearly 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured some US$30 billion into mainland China since a political thaw in the late 1980s.
